title: Monte Carlo null-model test
code_simulate:
set.seed(240505)
d <- data.frame(gene=1:80, on_X=rbinom(80, 1, .32))
write.csv(d, file.path(out_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
barplot(c(sum(d$on_X==0),sum(d$on_X==1)), names.arg=c("Autosomes", "X chromosome"),
        col=c("#9AA6AC","#146A85"), border=NA, ylab="Candidate genes")
code_analysis:
observed <- sum(d$on_X)
p0 <- .20; n <- nrow(d); B <- 9999
null <- rbinom(B, size=n, prob=p0)
p_value <- (1+sum(abs(null-n*p0)>=abs(observed-n*p0)))/(B+1)
result <- data.frame(observed_X=observed, expected_X=n*p0, monte_carlo_p=p_value)
biology: Test whether candidate sex-determination genes are unusually concentrated on the X chromosome.
design: A teaching null assigns independent genes to X with probability equal to its opportunity share.
data_characteristics: One binary chromosome class per gene
Test statistic: deviation in number on X
other_examples: Offspring under a specified segregation model
question: Is chromosome occupancy inconsistent with the specified opportunity model?
null: Each independent candidate gene has probability 0.20 of being on X.
options: Specify the biological null model before simulation.
Choose the statistic and one- or two-sided extremeness rule.
Increase B for finer Monte Carlo precision.
assumptions: The null opportunity model is biologically appropriate.
The simulation captures dependence; this simple example assumes independent genes.
parametric: For independent binary assignments, compare with an exact binomial test.
nonparametric: Randomize gene labels across eligible genomic positions when that matches the null.
generating_model: 80 independent Bernoulli indicators with true X probability 0.32. The tested null probability is 0.20; null simulation uses 9999 binomial draws.
generating_truth: The true occupancy probability is 0.32, so the tested 0.20 null is false.
teaching_point: A simulation test is only as useful as its biological null model.
practice: How would linked genes change the null simulation?
